title: Tai migrations into mainland Southeast Asia
summary: Tai-speaking peoples of the Yunnan plateau moved steadily into Southeast Asia over several centuries, spurred by the Nanchao state and then by a flood of migration after Kublai Khan’s conquest of it in 1253. By the thirteenth century they had reached Assam; the Shan of Burma and the Lao of the upper Mekong descend from them. Tradition dates the Tai kingdom of Sukhothai to 1238, and Lan Na at Chiang Mai to 1296.

uncertainty.note: The Library of Congress study says "over several centuries" from the mid-seventh century; the Bunkyo University paper says large-scale migration took place between the 7th and 13th centuries. Sources differ on the conquest of the Dali/Nanchao kingdom: 1253 (Library of Congress) and 1254 (Bunkyo paper). Sukhothai’s 1238 date is called a tradition.

beats.caption: Bands of Tai from Yunnan move steadily south into Southeast Asia over several centuries.
Kublai Khan’s armies conquer Nanchao in 1253; a flood of migration follows and Tai warriors reinforce Sukhothai against the Khmer.
Tai war parties found the kingdom of Lan Na at Chiang Mai in 1296; the Tai settle as Shan in Burma and Lao on the upper Mekong.

reviewer_note: Least sure: the id year 1250 is a midpoint; the migration spans centuries. The Dali conquest date differs between sources (1253 vs 1254). The Assam branch is mentioned in the summary but not pinned. Sukhothai is called a tradition by the source. Yunnan point is the Wikidata location of Yunnan, used as an anchor for the plateau.
